texts.text: The harbour at sunrise does not begin with light but with sound. Somewhere out past the breakwater the swell meets the shingle and drags back, a slow breathing that has been going on all night and will go on all day, and in the last blue hour before dawn it is the only thing awake. Then a gull lifts off the roof of the fish shed with an ungainly clatter and everything follows: a chain ticking against a mast, a door rolling open on a rusted rail, the first diesel coughing twice and settling into its long idle. The town is built of small sounds and it assembles itself out of them each morning in the same order, as if some patient hand were laying down bricks. The light comes sideways. Along the harbour wall the houses face east with the patient indifference of things that have been painted white for two hundred years, and the sea catches the sky before the land does, so the water goes pale first, a thin rinse of silver that spreads outward from the channel. The boats lift out of that flat grey as the light finds them: masts, then rigging, then the tangle of orange floats and blue barrels on the quay, and finally the hulls, black and red and one old green thing with a name half scrubbed off. Every window in the town begins to hold a small square of sky. The gulls turn and their bellies glow. On the front, the cafés are still shut, but the man who owns the corner one is out with a bucket and a mop, working the pavement in slow arcs that leave a darker, clean-smelling trail behind him. He stops to look at the water the way he does every morning and then goes back to work. Further along, a woman is arranging crates of bread on a trestle table, and the smell of that bread crosses the road and joins the salt and the diesel and the cold stone and the faint sweetness of whatever it was the tide brought in. A dog trots past on some urgent private business. The lamp posts, still lit, are losing their argument with the day and their pools of yellow shrink and vanish. The tide is going out. This is the great event of a harbour morning, though nobody speaks of it. It leaves the slipway streaked and shining and exposes the green weed on the lower steps, and it turns the inner basin into a place of mud and reflection where a dinghy sits stranded at an angle with its rope slack in the water. Farther out the sandbars show their backs. The water inside the walls is so still at this hour that the boats have two of everything, and the reflected masts point down into a second sky that is slightly greener and much more uncertain than the first. By now the fishing boats that went out before midnight are coming back. You hear them ahead of seeing them, a low note running under the gulls, and then they appear one behind another at the harbour mouth, low in the water and unhurried, trailing their wake in long curves that undo themselves slowly against the wall. The men on board are working even now, stacking, hosing, coiling. When the first one passes the light it throws up a brief shell of white spray that the sun turns into something

texts.text: Before any light arrives the harbour belongs to sound and to smell: the slap of a halyard against an aluminium mast, a rope creaking somewhere out in the dark, the flat mineral smell of weed and diesel and cold water, and under all of it the slow breathing of the tide working at the stone. The boats sit in their rows with their hulls colourless in that last hour, one lamp burning on a trawler where a man is already awake and moving about his deck with the patience of someone who has never once hurried at this hour. Nothing is quite still and nothing is quite moving. Then the sky begins to separate from the sea, and the separating is the first real event of the day. What had been one grey body of nothing divides along a line that is not drawn but implied, the water going the colour of a knife blade and the sky above it going pearl, then faintly green, then the palest possible rose. The gulls wake in that order, one voice first, thin and querulous, and then a dozen, and then the whole breakwater is loud with them. A cormorant crosses low and straight, going somewhere with the air of a man late for work. On the quay the fish market is already lit, and its lights are the only hard thing in a soft world: white strips under a corrugated roof, steam off the hoses, boxes of ice stacked in leaning towers, men in yellow oilskins standing with their hands in their pockets while the auctioneer murmurs into a microphone in the flat, unhurried, faintly bored voice of a man who has sold this same morning ten thousand times. The fish lie in their ruined silver, stiff and beautiful and entirely dead. Behind the quay the town begins to show itself, and it shows itself in the wrong order. First the roofs, because they are highest: slate gone purple with damp, a forest of chimneys, television aerials thin as drawing pins, the square church tower with its clock face still unreadable. Then the windows, lighting one by one as people get up, a slow irregular counting across the hill, and between two of those windows a baker's fan begins to turn and pushes a smell of hot bread all the way down to the water, where the gulls take an interest in it. And then the sun comes up. It does not rise so much as arrive, swelling out of the sea beyond the breakwater, and for perhaps four minutes the whole harbour is made of a material it will never be made of again: apricot and brass, the water turning over in slow coins of light, every wet surface braided with fire, the masts drawing long lines across the quay as though someone had ruled the morning with a pencil. The stone of the seawall goes the colour of honey. The white hulls go pink. A man on a ladder painting a boat's name stops, brush in the air, and looks at it, because it is worth looking at, and then goes back to the name. The water inside the harbour is not one thing but fifty: flat glass in the shelter of the inner basin, broken by a dinghy's wake into a shivering net of light, a petrol rainbow widening from an outboard, a brown roil where a mooring chain has dragged the mud, a hoop of bubbles where something fed. A pair of swans, absurd and ceremonial, move through all of it without disturbing anything. The reflections of the houses come apart and reassemble with each small swell, so that the town appears to be having a quiet argument with itself about where it is. Out at the harbour mouth a trawler gets under way, and the sound of it is the first engine of the day, a heavy satisfied thudding that carries across the water and sets every window in the town a little further alight. Its exhaust hangs in the cold air behind it, blue under a sky that is no longer blue, and its wake runs back to the wall in long folds that arrive with a soft slap, flick, slap, and set the moored boats nodding at one another like old men agreeing about the weather. The people come out then, in twos and threes and then in a trickle that becomes a stream: a woman in a red coat walking a dog that stops at every bollard, an old man carrying a bucket of lines and a knife with which he intends to do something decisive to a mackerel, two children in school uniform kicking a can along the seawall until it goes over the edge, a queue forming at the ferry slip for the boat that will not leave for forty minutes. Nobody is in a hurry and everybody is on their way somewhere. There are cats on the quay, of course, sitting in the attitude of small sphinxes beside the ice boxes, waiting for the inevitable. There are pilings bearded with weed and hung with old tyres. There is a noticeboard with a laminated tide table peeling at the corner, a life ring on a rail with a faded name stencilled on it, a coil of rope that has been coiled by the same hand for thirty years. At the bottom of the harbour steps the water is clear enough to see the stones and a single bright wrapper. By seven the light has hardened and the colours have gone ordinary, and the day becomes practical. Vans reverse onto the quay with a beeping that seems rude after so much quiet. Crates go up and crates come down. A café on the corner puts out its board and takes in its chairs, and the first coffee of the morning is poured into a cup that has been warmed, by a woman who has done this ten thousand times too and who looks out at the water as she does it, checking the weather on behalf of everyone. The clock in the tower finally becomes readable, and the harbour master unlocks his office, and the flag goes up the pole in a series of little flaps. A bell rings somewhere behind the houses. A radio plays in a shed. All of it is a machine that has been running for six hundred years and will run again tomorrow, and the sunrise, which was the most beautiful thing in the world for four minutes, has become ordinary weather, useful for drying nets and judging wind. The sun clears the breakwater entirely and the harbour is simply a harbour again: bright, busy, slightly shabby, smelling of fish and salt and hot pastry and diesel, gulls screaming, a dog barking, a man laughing at something on the other side of the water. The light lies flat and white on everything and asks nothing of anybody. Whatever there was of the morning's other world has gone into the stone, which is warm now if you put your hand on it, and which will hold it until evening. --- TEST branch: this branch starts from turn 6 — your 1,200-word harbour-town request (my reply #6) — and yes, I can see all the earlier messages: the greeting, the plain-text yes/no question, the Aico ask and your "Yes, explore first", the folder report, and the 1–400 list.
